title: How To Get The Truth From Untruthful Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/11/13/how-to-get-the-truth-from-untruthful-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a specific interrogation technique - the "why strategy" - for quickly getting truthful answers from students accused of misbehavior that the teacher did not personally witness. The six-step method involves keeping the reporting student's information confidential, waiting roughly thirty minutes so the accused student believes the incident has been forgotten, approaching them by surprise rather than with warning, projecting an assumption of already knowing the facts, and then asking a "why" question ("why did you push Brian?") rather than the more common "did you" question, since students are conditioned to reflexively deny "did you" accusations but are caught off guard by a "why" framing. He explains that the student's immediate reaction to the why question - confusion versus panic - reliably reveals guilt or innocence within seconds. A closing note clarifies the technique is meant only for secondhand reports, not incidents the teacher personally witnessed.
points: The "why strategy" is designed specifically for secondhand reports of misbehavior the teacher didn't personally witness.
Waiting about thirty minutes before confronting the accused student increases the element of surprise.
Asking "why did you..." instead of "did you..." catches students off guard, since they're conditioned to deny direct accusations reflexively.
The student's immediate emotional reaction to the why question reliably signals guilt or innocence within seconds.
The technique is explicitly not intended for incidents the teacher personally witnessed.
quotes: Getting to the truth, though, can be difficult. Backed into a corner, confronted with a report of misbehavior, students are often untruthful.
The why strategy is a way to cut through the deception and get to the truth quickly, so you can get on with the business of teaching.
It's best if the accused (Karla) isn't aware you know anything about the reported incident.
Allow some time to pass before confronting the accused student—at least 30 minutes.
Most teachers will ask a did you question. As in, “Karla, did you push Brian?” But dishonest students are conditioned to lie as soon as the words “did you” begin tumbling out of your mouth.
You, however, are going to ask a why question—which they’re unprepared for. “Hey Karla, why did you push Brian on the way out to recess?
It can turn a potentially frustrating, stressful, and lengthy situation into a 15-second conversation.
